\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than the current literature assumes.
We demonstrated three pitfalls that undermine standard approaches: method choice alone swings FDR significance from 100\% to 25\% ($\kappa{=}0.185$), first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 24/24 to 0/8 significant pairs across contamination levels.
These findings establish that single-method, single-regime analyses---the current default---cannot reliably distinguish genuine temporal precedence from statistical artifacts.

Our multi-method consensus framework addresses this fragility by requiring convergent evidence across ${\geq}4/5$ independent methods and ${\geq}3/4$ random seeds.
Calibrated on built-in experimental controls, the framework achieves 0\% false positive rate at the null control ($\alpha{=}0.0$, single seed) and 0\% false negative rate against effect-size reference pairs at full contamination ($\alpha{=}1.0$), with four tiers of practical guidance scaling from exploratory screening to publication-grade claims.

Applying the framework yields a concrete finding: token entropy serves as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (with preliminary single-seed evidence at $\alpha{=}0.75$), with $|r|{>}0.99$ and complete directional asymmetry (0/24 reverse-direction FDR-significant pairs).
This result is deliberately scoped to lexical diversity, not model collapse broadly, since the perplexity channel proved entirely spurious under differencing.

The methodological pitfalls we expose are not specific to our experimental setting---they arise from generic properties of short, non-stationary time series---and we conjecture the consensus framework transfers to other iterative training settings where multiple detection methods can be applied in parallel.
Limitations are detailed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}; future directions are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.

\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
Token entropy Granger-precedes distinct-1 and distinct-2 with a consistent one-generation lead.
Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0).
Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), confirming directional asymmetry.

\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, single seed).}
At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (seed=42), three of four forward-direction pairs reach FDR significance: ECE$\to$distinct-1 ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.046$), ECE$\to$distinct-2 ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.046$), and token entropy$\to$distinct-2 ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.048$).
Token entropy$\to$distinct-1 is borderline ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.054$).
All four reverse directions are non-significant ($p{>}0.49$).
These single-seed results require multi-seed confirmation before serving as primary evidence.

\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
ECE performs equivalently to token entropy across four of five methods (naive, differenced, threshold, permutation Granger).
Its classification as ``secondary'' is driven entirely by Toda--Yamamoto Type~II errors at $T{=}10$, where bootstrap power analysis yields estimated power of 0.05--0.20 depending on $d_{\max}$.
Resolving ECE's true canary status requires longer time series.

\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
Not all metrics serve as canaries.
Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Training language models on their own output across successive generations leads to progressive distribution degradation, a phenomenon variously termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse} or Model Autophagy Disorder~\cite{alemohammad2024mad}.
Tail modes vanish, lexical diversity narrows, and calibration deteriorates as each generation's output becomes the next generation's training data.
As large language models become ubiquitous content generators, the fraction of machine-generated text on the web grows steadily, making iterative training collapse---where models are unwittingly trained on the output of earlier model generations---a practical concern for the long-term stability of language model ecosystems.

A natural follow-up question is whether cheap-to-compute statistics---\emph{canary metrics}---can provide early warning of impending collapse, analogous to early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological and climate systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}.
Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} informally observe that expected calibration error rises before accuracy degrades; SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators of distributional shift; and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.
Yet the statistical methodology underlying these lead-lag claims---whether a canary metric genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation, or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends---has received little scrutiny.

We identify several methodological deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse:
(1)~no differencing tests to rule out spurious regression arising from shared non-stationary trends---a well-known hazard when correlating co-trending time series;
(2)~no multi-method cross-validation---conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose implicit assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined;
(3)~no multiple comparison correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg FDR control), increasing the risk of false discoveries when testing many metric pairs simultaneously; and
(4)~no regime-dependent analysis, despite the possibility that the same statistical test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
Their analysis, however, is limited to a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and reports informal visual comparisons without statistical tests---leaving open the question of whether the observed lead is genuine or an artifact of shared trends.
The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}---widely adopted in ecology for anticipating tipping points---provides the theoretical motivation for canary-based prediction, but has not been systematically applied to iterative training collapse with the methodological rigor that short, noisy time series demand~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

We address these gaps through a systematic case study of canary prediction of diversity collapse---the progressive loss of lexical diversity in model-generated text across training generations.
Using Pythia-410M across five contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we expose three methodological pitfalls that undermine naive lead-lag analysis:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Method sensitivity.} Applied to the same data (16 candidate canary$\to$downstream pairs, including candidates later excluded; \S\ref{sec:case_study}), five lead-lag detection methods yield FDR significance rates ranging from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 25\% (Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality), with inter-method agreement of Cohen's $\kappa{=}0.185$ (poor agreement).
    \item \textbf{Spurious regression.} Canary$\to$perplexity associations appear near-universal in undifferenced analysis but vanish entirely after first-differencing ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), revealing them as artifacts of co-trending rather than genuine temporal precedence.
    \item \textbf{Regime dependence.} Permutation Granger tests find 24/24 canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant at full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$) but 0/8 at $\alpha{\leq}0.50$, demonstrating that detectability depends sharply on the contamination level.
\end{enumerate}
To move beyond single-method analysis, we propose a multi-method consensus framework with empirically calibrated thresholds, requiring agreement across multiple independent statistical methods and random seeds before classifying a lead-lag relationship as robust.

The framework's utility is demonstrated by its calibration on built-in experimental controls.
Naive cross-correlation identifies 100\% of canary--collapse metric pairs as FDR-significant; the consensus pipeline (requiring ${\geq}4/5$ methods and ${\geq}3/4$ seeds) retains only those pairs meeting effect-size criteria calibrated against the null control.
On reference extremes, the framework achieves a false positive rate of 0\% at the $\alpha{=}0.0$ null control (single seed) (where individual methods reach up to 100\% FPR) and a false negative rate of 0\% against six effect-size reference pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
Applying the framework, we identify token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$, validated by the full consensus pipeline, with cross-correlation $|r|{>}0.99$ and directional asymmetry confirmed by 0/24 reverse-direction FDR-significant pairs; preliminary single-seed evidence at $\alpha{=}0.75$ awaits multi-seed confirmation.
We note that Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Systematic exposure of three methodological pitfalls} in lead-lag analysis of iterative training collapse.
    We quantify each pitfall: method choice alone swings significance from 100\% to 25\% with a spurious-signal rate of 62.5\% (75\% including the underpowered Toda--Yamamoto test); first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely; and the same Granger test shifts from 24/24 FDR-significant pairs to 0/8 across contamination levels.
    These results demonstrate that single-method, single-regime analyses---the current norm in this literature---are unreliable.

    \item \textbf{A multi-method consensus framework} that instantiates known statistical methods in a novel sequential pipeline with empirical calibration, offering four-tier practical guidance ranging from exploratory ($K{\geq}1/5$) to conservative ($K{=}5/5$).
    The framework achieves FPR${=}$0\% (single seed at $\alpha{=}0.0$) and FNR${=}$0\% on reference extremes, providing robustness against miscalibration of any individual method.

    \item \textbf{Application of the framework to identify token entropy} as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (with preliminary single-seed evidence at $\alpha{=}0.75$), scoped precisely to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$) rather than model collapse broadly, with a tiered practical guide mapping contamination regimes to recommended analysis strategies.
\end{enumerate}

\S\ref{sec:related_work} surveys related work on model collapse, early-warning signals, and lead-lag methodology.
\S\ref{sec:background} establishes the formal setup, notation, and the five detection methods used throughout.
\S\ref{sec:method} distills the three methodological pitfalls into a unified diagnostic framework, presents the multi-method consensus pipeline, and reports its empirical calibration.
\S\ref{sec:experiments} provides full experimental results: method sensitivity analysis (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), regime-dependent detectability (\S\ref{sec:regime}), a case study of canary prediction of diversity collapse (\S\ref{sec:case_study}), and consensus framework validation (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications---including the practical utility paradox, the token entropy--perplexity distinction, and NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis---and outlines directions for future work.
\S\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes, followed by a dedicated Limitations section (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and five contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
The consensus framework's structure---multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication---is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds) are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates at these thresholds.
Preliminary cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (single seed, $\alpha{=}1.0$) replicates the entropy-leads-diversity pattern at Tier~3 consensus: all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach $K{\geq}4/5$ method agreement (permutation Granger $p_{\text{FDR}}{=}0.003$), with 0/6 reverse-direction pairs significant.
Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.

\paragraph{FPR/FNR calibration asymmetry.}
The FPR and FNR estimates in our calibration analysis differ in their coverage of the seed dimension.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process---such as a latent distributional shift in the training data---could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.

\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and five contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
The consensus framework's structure---multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication---is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds) are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates at these thresholds.
Preliminary cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (single seed, $\alpha{=}1.0$) replicates the entropy-leads-diversity pattern at Tier~3 consensus: all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach $K{\geq}4/5$ method agreement (permutation Granger $p_{\text{FDR}}{=}0.003$), with 0/6 reverse-direction pairs significant.
Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium likewise yields 0/8 pairs at Confirmatory consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$), matching the Pythia result and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across architectures.
Notably, GPT-2-medium exhibits substantially stronger canary drift at this contamination level (entropy: $-32.8\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$)---likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step---yet diversity decline is milder ($-23.5\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$).
The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.

\paragraph{FPR/FNR calibration asymmetry.}
The FPR and FNR estimates in our calibration analysis differ in their coverage of the seed dimension.
FPR is validated on the method dimension only, using a single seed at the null-control condition ($\alpha{=}0.0$).
FNR is validated on the joint method${\times}$seed dimension, aggregating across four seeds at full contamination ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
This asymmetry means our FPR estimate of 0\% may be optimistic: if seed-level variance in false positive rates is non-negligible, the true FPR under the consensus rule could exceed zero.
Full joint calibration---requiring multi-seed null-control experiments at $\alpha{=}0.0$---remains an open direction for future work.

\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure's elevated FNR (33.3\%, missing 2 of 6 directional pairs) is attributable to insufficient residual degrees of freedom at this series length, not to a fundamental deficiency in the method itself.
This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$.
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure produces valid test statistics at all window lengths ($T \in \{5, \ldots, 10\}$), but with unstable sensitivity---3/6 to 6/6 pairs reach significance depending on window length---confirming that its elevated FNR reflects limited residual degrees of freedom rather than absence of signal.

\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method consensus: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.

\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse---but at these contamination levels, degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
At $\alpha{\leq}0.50$, where early warning would be most valuable, the canary signal is undetectable by any method tested.
This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards---tracking cumulative trend shifts across many generations---than to single-point threshold alarms.
If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.

\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data}---measuring the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text---while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text}---measuring the model's self-consistency on its own outputs.
The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}---both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.

\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods and explains the Toda--Yamamoto procedure's poor power in our setting.
Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to---rather than replacement for---traditional significance testing.

\paragraph{Future work.}
Several directions extend this work.
Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
Cross-architecture validation beyond our preliminary single-seed GPT-2-medium result requires multi-seed replication; evaluation on larger-scale models would further test generalizability.
Online monitoring---integrating canary metrics into training pipelines for real-time collapse detection---is a natural applied extension.
Accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking} would test whether canary dynamics differ from the replace-mode setting studied here.
Finally, connecting the empirically observed detectability boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.50$--$0.75$ to theoretical phase transition analysis~\cite{truong2025entropy} could yield a principled explanation for why canary signals emerge at this contamination regime rather than at lower contamination levels.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than the current literature assumes.
Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to 62.5\%, first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious, and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 24/24 to 0/8 significant pairs across contamination levels.
These pitfalls establish that single-method, single-regime analyses---the current default---cannot reliably distinguish genuine temporal precedence from statistical artifacts.

Our multi-method consensus framework addresses this fragility by requiring convergent evidence across multiple independent methods and random seeds.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Training language models on their own output across successive generations leads to progressive distribution degradation, a phenomenon variously termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse} or Model Autophagy Disorder~\cite{alemohammad2024mad}.
Tail modes vanish, lexical diversity narrows, and calibration deteriorates as each generation's output becomes the next generation's training data.
As large language models become ubiquitous content generators, the fraction of machine-generated text on the web grows steadily, making iterative training collapse---where models are unwittingly trained on the output of earlier model generations---a practical concern for the long-term stability of language model ecosystems.

A natural follow-up question is whether cheap-to-compute statistics---\emph{canary metrics}---can provide early warning of impending collapse, analogous to early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological and climate systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}.
Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} informally observe that expected calibration error rises before accuracy degrades; SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators of distributional shift; and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.
Yet the statistical methodology underlying these lead-lag claims---whether a canary metric genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation, or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends---has received little scrutiny.

We identify several methodological deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse:
(1)~no differencing tests to rule out spurious regression arising from shared non-stationary trends---a well-known hazard when correlating co-trending time series;
(2)~no multi-method cross-validation---conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose implicit assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined;
(3)~no multiple comparison correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg FDR control), increasing the risk of false discoveries when testing many metric pairs simultaneously; and
(4)~no regime-dependent analysis, despite the possibility that the same statistical test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
Their analysis, however, is limited to a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and reports informal visual comparisons without statistical tests---leaving open the question of whether the observed lead is genuine or an artifact of shared trends.
The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}---widely adopted in ecology for anticipating tipping points---provides the theoretical motivation for canary-based prediction, but has not been systematically applied to iterative training collapse with the methodological rigor that short, noisy time series demand~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

We address these gaps through a systematic case study of canary prediction of diversity collapse---the progressive loss of lexical diversity in model-generated text across training generations.
Using Pythia-410M across five contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we expose three methodological pitfalls that undermine naive lead-lag analysis:

    \item \textbf{Regime dependence.} Permutation Granger tests find 24/24 canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant at full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$) but 0/8 at $\alpha{\leq}0.50$, demonstrating that detectability depends sharply on the contamination level.
\end{enumerate}
To move beyond single-method analysis, we propose a multi-method consensus framework with empirically calibrated thresholds, requiring agreement across multiple independent statistical methods and random seeds before classifying a lead-lag relationship as robust.

The framework's utility is demonstrated by its calibration on built-in experimental controls.
Naive cross-correlation identifies 100\% of canary--collapse metric pairs as FDR-significant; the consensus pipeline (requiring ${\geq}4/5$ methods and ${\geq}3/4$ seeds) retains only those pairs meeting effect-size criteria calibrated against the null control.

We note that Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}.

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Systematic exposure of three methodological pitfalls} (method sensitivity, spurious regression, regime dependence) in lead-lag analysis of iterative training collapse.

    \item \textbf{A multi-method consensus framework} that instantiates known statistical methods in a novel sequential pipeline with empirical calibration, achieving FNR${=}$0\% on effect-size reference pairs (4-method panel, permutation Granger power${=}1.0$) with four-tier practical guidance.

    \item \textbf{Identification of token entropy as a robust one-generation-ahead canary} for diversity collapse at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, confirmed by 4 independent methods, 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium, with complete directional asymmetry (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse). The claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.
\end{enumerate}

\S\ref{sec:related_work} surveys related work on model collapse, early-warning signals, and lead-lag methodology.
\S\ref{sec:background} establishes the formal setup, notation, and the five detection methods used throughout.
\S\ref{sec:method} distills the three methodological pitfalls into a unified diagnostic framework, presents the multi-method consensus pipeline, and reports its empirical calibration.
\S\ref{sec:experiments} provides full experimental results: method sensitivity analysis (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), regime-dependent detectability (\S\ref{sec:regime}), a case study of canary prediction of diversity collapse (\S\ref{sec:case_study}), and consensus framework validation (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications---including the practical utility paradox, the token entropy--perplexity distinction, and NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis---and outlines directions for future work.
\S\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes, followed by a dedicated Limitations section (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than the current literature assumes.
Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to 62.5\%, first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious, and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 24/24 to 0/8 significant pairs across contamination levels.
These pitfalls establish that single-method, single-regime analyses---the current default---cannot reliably distinguish genuine temporal precedence from statistical artifacts.

Our multi-method consensus framework addresses this fragility by requiring convergent evidence across multiple independent methods and random seeds.
Calibrated on effect-size reference pairs with a non-circular 4-method panel, the framework achieves FNR${=}$0\% with permutation Granger power${=}1.0$, and four tiers of practical guidance scaling from exploratory screening to publication-grade claims.

Applying the framework, token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, confirmed by 4 independent methods, 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium, with complete directional asymmetry (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) and a consistent one-generation lead.
This finding is deliberately scoped to lexical diversity, not model collapse broadly, since the perplexity channel proved entirely spurious under differencing.

The methodological pitfalls we expose arise from generic properties of short, non-stationary time series, and we conjecture the consensus framework transfers to other iterative training settings where multiple detection methods can be applied in parallel.
Limitations are detailed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}; future directions are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter autoregressive language model.
Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across five contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.

We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha{=}0.25$ uses three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; other conditions use seed~42.

We track two \emph{canary metrics}---cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}---and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
